content: The periodate ion exists in two forms: IO₄⁻ (metaperiodate) and IO₆⁵⁻ (orthoperiodate). These ions are derived from periodic acid. Compounds containing these ions are referred to as periodates. It is important to note that the correct pronunciation is per-eye-oh-date, not period-ate. Examples of periodates include sodium periodate (NaIO₄) and potassium periodate (KIO₄). For a more extensive list of periodates, refer to the relevant category. Periodates can exist in two structural forms. The metaperiodate ion is represented as IO₄⁻, while the orthoperiodate ion is represented as IO₆⁵⁻. Compounds containing these ions are classified as either metaperiodates or orthoperiodates, but they are commonly referred to collectively as periodates. Under neutral or weakly acidic conditions, IO₄⁻ is the predominant species, existing in equilibrium with a smaller amount of H₄IO₆⁻. In basic conditions, H₃IO₆²⁻ is formed, along with other ionic species. Iodine, like its periodic table neighbor tellurium, tends to exhibit hexacoordination. This results in the formation of units such as HₙIO₆⁵⁻ⁿ, which are relatively common. However, in the case of iodine, tetracoordinate units like IO₄⁻ are also frequently observed. Periodates have the ability to cleave carbon-carbon bonds when both carbon atoms are bonded to oxygen atoms, either in the form of hydroxyl (-OH) or carbonyl (C=O) groups. This property is particularly useful in molecular biochemistry, where periodates are employed to modify saccharide rings. This is because many fiveand six-membered sugars often contain vicinal diols, which are susceptible to cleavage by periodates.
